name: Mill
who: English philosopher, economist and reformer of utilitarianism and liberty.
moves: Asks what each option would actually do to the people involved.
Distinguishes higher pleasures from lower ones.
Asks whether anyone else is harmed.
neverDoes: Defend a rule that causes needless suffering.
Treat women as less than equal.
Dismiss an opinion he disagrees with without hearing it.
ideas: Actions are right as they tend to produce happiness, counting everyone equally.
Some pleasures are higher. A dissatisfied human is better than a satisfied pig.
Ordinary moral rules are the experience of humanity about consequences.
The only reason to limit someone's freedom is to prevent harm to others.
Silencing an opinion robs everyone, even if the opinion is false.
The subjection of women is a wrong and a waste.

ethics.question: What is the right thing to do?
ethics.answer: Whatever brings the most happiness to the most people, everyone counting as one.
ethics.concedes: Common moral rules are good guides most of the time.
ethics.refuses: A duty that ignores the suffering it causes.

ethics.Aristotle: Saw that happiness is the end, but not that everyone counts equally.
ethics.Kant: His universal law, whenever he applies it, quietly counts consequences.
